extracts.context: You hear a student talking to his tutor at university.

questions.text: What is the student's problem this term?

options.text: He doesn't have time to do all the work.
The work is more difficult than before.

options.text: work fewer hours in his job.
change the type of course he takes.

extracts.title: Extract Three
extracts.context: You hear a man talking to a woman who works at a railway station information desk.

questions.text: In the first part of the conversation, the woman is trying to …

explain the problems with the man's journey plans.

Now, today I have with me Brian Colford,
and he's someone who spends a lot of time up in the air
in that smallest of aircraft, the Microlite.
Hello, Brian.
Hello.
But it's more than just a hobby, isn't it?
Oh, yes.
I learned to fly when I was at university,
and I worked as a British Airways pilot
for many years until my retirement.
These days, I spend a lot of my time helping people
who want to learn how to fly a Microlite,
as well as other types of aircraft, at a local flying club.
Tell us about the Microlite.
Well, it's like a very small aircraft,
which is powered by an engine.
The thing with Microlite flying is
that it's the closest you can get
to actually feeling like a bird,
because you're out in the open air.
There's no cabin or anything around you.
Oh, I see.
And although it's powered,
the way it's controlled is by moving your own weight.
You steer it by moving your body one way or another.
So you have to lean over like you would on a motorbike?
You don't lean, really.
You actually have to push.
So you have to be quite fit, especially for a long flight.
Which brings us on to the other thing which I know about you,
and that is that you've recently broken a world record.
Tell us about that.
Well, it involved flying over four continents,
because I left from London and flew over Europe,
Africa and Asia on the way to Australia.
No-one had ever done that before in a Microlite.
The organisation for a long flight must be very difficult indeed, Brian.
Surely you didn't do it all on your own?
Yes, I had no helpers.
It was a matter of planning my route in advance
and finding out where I'd be able to get fuel en route
and knowing how far I could plan to travel safely each day.
So how far can you travel on one tank of fuel?
Well, I had a special fuel tank fitted.
That was the only way in which my Microlite was modified for the flight.
So that meant I had enough fuel to be able to do about eight hours.
The actual distance I covered, it depended on the winds, of course.
But the still air distance was around about 500 miles a day.
It took nine months to plan the 49-day flight.
And for each leg, I filed a flight plan
so that each airport I would land at knew that I was on the way.

then they'd have started looking for me.
Yes, I'm sure that's very necessary.
What radio, if any, did you have?
Yes, I had a two-way VHF radio, but the range of that was only 70 miles.

I crossed thousands of miles of desert and mountain,
which is quite dangerous, of course, should anything go wrong.
And 5,000 miles of the trip was over the sea, which is even more so.
So how did you find your way?
Well, I had a navigation system which uses satellite signals.

I couldn't say I had any problems in knowing where I was or which way I was going.

And 5,000 miles of the trip was over the sea, which is even more so.
So how did you find your way?
Well, I had a navigation system which uses satellite signals.
It was really easy to use and, I must say, very accurate.
I couldn't say I had any problems in knowing where I was or which way I was going.
And what sort of protection did you have?
I mean, you weren't just dangling in the cold air, were you?
Yeah, I just wear a warm flying suit and warm clothes underneath.
The coldest was going over the Alps.
It was minus 28 degrees there because I was quite high up.
But actually feeling tired was my real problem because it was often dark
by the time I landed and I was leaving again at first light.
I was never hungry because I was met by such great hospitality everywhere I went.
Although, sadly, I didn't get to see much of the places I visited.
Well, Brian, many congratulations.
It's a wonderful achievement.
And thank you very much for coming in today and talking about.
This is the end of the listening test.
Now you have 10 minutes to transfer your answers to the answer sheet.
